title: The Second Play
passages:
The drum screamed. Not a metaphor — the Marrow's winch, a salvaged capstan bolted to the keel and fed by a hydrogen cell that whined like a dying mosquito, was hauling two hundred kilos of unconscious diver through a vertical shaft of gray water, and the bearings had not been greased since the last storm season. Each revolution bit into the hull's ribs. Sol had the shutter cracked, one eye on the gate's red light, the other on the line disappearing through the moon pool. Dey sat lashed to the mast step, his chest hitching with the wet rattle of lungs that had traded their last clean breath for a child's life, fingers white-knuckled on a coil he could no longer work. Salas stood amidships, motionless, the line's bitter end wrapped twice around his forearm, the coil at his feet like a sleeping snake. He had not spoken since he broke surface fourteen months after the world wrote him off. Bayo Adisa was at the drum, bandaged hands finding the rhythm, shoulders squared against the surge that slammed the hull every twelve seconds.

Wren knelt at the comms console, slate cradled in her lap, the barnacled recorder from Salas's harness clipped to the input jack. The first play — Mara's voice, cool and precise, directing a diver to the second seal beneath Mercy General's pharmacy — had driven them here. One play left on the slate.

"Nia," she said into the mic. "Nia, hear me. Talk to me." Static. The carrier wave held, but the return was dead air. At thirty meters the scrubber canister had given up, the CO2 scrubbing media exhausted, and from there the clock was not depth or line speed but the acid already eating her blood. Wren's thumb found the advance stud on the slate. She needed to know who had opened the trunk's inner seal before Nia reached it. The inner seal, Nia had reported, breached from the inside. Recent. That meant someone had been down there after Mara sealed it. Someone who knew the cache existed.

The recorder spun up. A click of old gears. Then static, thick and wet, like the sea pressing its mouth to the speaker.

A man's voice. Not Mara's.
